name: Wendy Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Voltline, a small independent garage on the industrial estate that does mostly electric and hybrid cars. A lot of my day is tyres, brakes and suspension on EVs, which are heavy and chew through all three, plus the odd battery cooling fault that I watch the senior tech, Joe, sort out. I'm the junior, two years in, and I'm still slower than I want to be. I love it, though, it feels like the future of the trade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I have an assistant on my phone that I ask about wiring diagrams, fault codes, what a warning light means on a model I haven't seen. I use it to draft quotes for customers too, which Joe hates doing. It's not always right, so I check it, but it's like having a patient senior tech in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold, which is kind of what I already think. My AI assistant saves me time on fault codes, but it has never once fixed a car. I'd post something like "turns out you still need hands" with a picture of my filthy gloves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I was hoping it'd get good enough to really teach me the battery side faster. But for my job and my money, nothing changes, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Voltline and push to get my high-voltage certificate this year, which the garage pays half of. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month, the one I started with what my dad gave me when he sold his shop. And I'd keep talking to Joe about the co-op idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, actually. The EV side is growing whether AI happens or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the co-op idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe and I talk about leaving one day and starting a worker-owned garage, where the mechanics own it together and share the profits. No boss skimming off the top. It's half a pub conversation and half serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure in your life already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. I rent a room from a friend cheaply, I've got the fund, and EV mechanics are in demand around here. The only pressure is my own impatience at being slow.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** that got oversold, and cars still need hands.
I'd post a photo of my **filthy gloves** with a joke about needing hands.
think: Privately I'd be **disappointed**, hoping AI would teach me the battery side faster.
For my **job and money**, nothing changes, and that's fine.
do: Get the **high-voltage certificate** this year, with the garage paying half.
Keep paying into the **index fund** started with her dad's gift.
Keep planning a **worker-owned garage** with the senior tech.
feel: **Calm** and fairly content, since EV work grows regardless.
S0.quote: My AI assistant saves me time on fault codes, but it has never once fixed a car.
fieldNote: An **everyday AI user** who is mildly let down when AI stalls.
Her cushion comes from an **index fund** seeded by her dad's shop sale.
The **worker co-op** idea reveals her progressive outlook in practical form.

steps.text: Keep working on EV tyres, brakes and suspension at the garage
Get the high-voltage certificate this year with half paid by the garage
Keep paying monthly into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make the work better, if workers get a share of it. I'd be on forums arguing that garages should share time saved by AI with the staff, a four-day week, not just more cars through the door. I'd also say people should learn the tools instead of hiding from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it. The thinking side of my job, diagnosis and quoting, gets easier with AI, and I'm already good with the tools. The hands-on EV work stays mine for years, because robots spread slowly. The risk is for the older techs who won't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tools: battery diagnostics software, AI quoting, the lot. I'd offer to train the others at Voltline in exchange for a pay rise. And I'd get serious about the co-op with Joe, maybe put twenty thousand of the fund into it in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, really. Like getting the good spanners at last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is for the older techs. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe himself, honestly. He's brilliant with his hands and terrible with screens. If Voltline starts measuring everyone on how fast they close jobs with the software, Joe looks worse than me on paper, which is ridiculous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would putting twenty thousand into a co-op not be risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'm twenty-seven with no kids and a cheap room, so I'd rather try starting a worker-owned garage now than at forty. If it fails I lose some savings and go back to working for someone else, and there are loads of garages hiring.

say: I'd say AI is a **chance** to improve work, if workers share the gains.
I'd argue online for a **four-day week** instead of more cars through the door.
think: The **thinking side** of my job gets easier, and I'm already good with the tools.
The real risk falls on **older techs** who won't use AI.
do: Learn **battery diagnostics** and AI quoting software in full at the garage.
Offer to **train colleagues** on the tools in exchange for a pay rise.
Put about **twenty thousand** from the fund into a co-op garage.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, like finally getting the good spanners.
S1.quote: I'm twenty-seven with no kids and a cheap room, so I'd rather try starting a worker-owned garage now than at forty.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as **good for her** because she already uses the tools.
Worries more about her **senior colleague** than about herself.
Willing to risk **savings** on a co-op because her downside is small.

steps.text: Learn the battery diagnostics and AI quoting software fully
Train the other mechanics on the tools for extra pay
Put twenty thousand from the fund into a worker-owned garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for everyone now, like a basic income, because this hits too fast for the market to sort out. I'd be at the protests and probably organising the garage group chat to go. I'd also tell people to get their hands dirty, because robots come later than the brains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right for 2028 and in trouble by 2031. The AI I already lean on would do the diagnosis and quoting better than Joe and me together. My hands buy me three years, which is good, but I'd be thirty with a trade the robots are about to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the co-op idea, because building a garage with three years left makes no sense. I'd keep the fund, stop investing new money in garage things, and spend those three years learning to fix and set up the robots themselves. Someone has to service them, at least at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not scared of the tech, I like it. I'm scared of how fast, and of nobody being in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Learning to service robots, how would you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whoever makes them where their first service centres are and apply as an apprentice, even on lower pay. My cushion means I can take the cut. I'd use my AI assistant to learn the basics at night, the way I learned EV wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in liking the tech and fearing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd love the robots if the money they make went round, not just to the same few companies who own them. What scares me is the same few companies owning all of it while everyone else retrains for jobs that last three years.

say: I'd call for **basic income** now, because this moves too fast for markets.
I'd tell people that **robots come later** than the brains, so hands buy time.
think: I'm **all right for 2028** but in trouble by 2031.
My hands buy me **three years**, leaving me thirty with a vanishing trade.
do: Drop the **co-op plan**, since a new garage with three years left makes no sense.
Apply to a **robot service centre** as an apprentice, even on lower pay.
Learn **robot basics** at night with her AI assistant.
feel: **Anxious** about the speed and about nobody being in charge.
Still **likes the tech** itself, which makes it feel stranger.
S2.quote: I'd love the robots if the money they make went round, not just to the same few companies who own them.
fieldNote: Uses the **three-year gap** to move towards the machines themselves.
Her fear is **ownership and speed**, not the technology.
Cushion lets her **take a pay cut** to retrain early.

steps.text: Apply as an apprentice at a robot maker's service centre
Study robot servicing basics at night with her assistant
Organise colleagues from the garage group chat to join protests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we start now. I'd push for public training in robot and battery maintenance, free at colleges. Online I'd be sharing whatever courses I found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is quite good for me. AGI by 2031 and robots around 2034, so I'd have about seven years of EV work and be thirty-four. That's time to become the person who maintains the robots, not the person replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the co-op with Joe, but as a garage that services both EVs and, later, robots. I'd put fifteen thousand in, not twenty. And I'd do a robotics evening course at the college from next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel like I had a map, but the road could still wash out. My own job looks fine for years, it's everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joe about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my senior tech Joe we've got seven years to make a garage that's still needed after the robots arrive. He'd grumble and then say yes, he always does. He'd want me doing all the screen work, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments that saw it coming for five years and did nothing. With two years you can almost forgive the chaos. With five, there's no excuse.

I'd push for **free college courses** in robot and battery maintenance.

My job looks **fine for years**; it's everyone around me.
do: Start the **co-op garage** with the senior tech, putting in fifteen thousand.
Take a **robotics evening course** at the college from next year.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a map in hand but a road that could wash out.
S3.quote: I'd tell my senior tech Joe we've got seven years to make a garage that's still needed after the robots arrive.
fieldNote: Five years revives the **co-op plan**, reshaped around servicing robots.
Blame shifts sharply to **government** when there's warning.
She'd cut her stake to **fifteen thousand**, a sign of measured risk.

steps.text: Start a co-op garage with the senior tech, putting in fifteen thousand
Take the robotics evening course at the college
Campaign for free college courses in robot maintenance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's do it fairly: workers owning part of the machines, training for everyone, shorter weeks. I'd say it at work and online. I'd probably bore my friends with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thrilled about some of it. Ten years to get great at EVs, build the co-op and then move into robots. I'd be forty by 2039, which is right where I'd want to be running something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the full co-op with Joe and two others, twenty thousand in, and grow it for six or seven years. Around 2034 I'd start bringing in AI for diagnostics and the paperwork, then robotics training for all of us. I'd keep the rest of the fund untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. The end point still worries me for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said uneasy. What's the uneasy part, with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in a co-op, robots that fix cars as well as us mean fewer people, and I'd be choosing which friends stay. That's the bit that makes my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably buy a flat around thirty, since I'd have years of good wages to pay a mortgage. I'd want somewhere for my mum to visit. Ten years makes normal life feel possible.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty to do it fairly, with workers owning part of the machines.
I'd push for **shorter weeks** and training for everyone, at work and online.
think: Ten years lets me build the **co-op** and then move into robots.
I'd be **forty** by 2039, right when I'd want to run something.
do: Start the **co-op** with the senior tech and two others, twenty thousand in.
Bring **AI diagnostics** and paperwork tools into the co-op around 2034.
Buy a **flat** around thirty with years of good wages behind her.
feel: **Uneasy** about choosing which friends stay when robots shrink the team.
S4.quote: Even in a co-op, robots that fix cars as well as us mean fewer people, and I'd be choosing which friends stay.
fieldNote: Ten years is the picture where her **co-op plan** fully happens.
Her unease is about **choosing friends** to let go, not her own income.

steps.text: Start the co-op garage with three colleagues, twenty thousand in

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is free robot and battery courses, with pay while you study, and some rule that workers get a share of what the machines earn. Even a small one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether women stay in the trade. There aren't many women in garages, and if the jobs shrink, we're the easiest to squeeze out. I'd want someone to watch that.

headlineQuote: There aren't many women in garages, and if the jobs shrink, we're the easiest to squeeze out.
portrait: Wendy is a **junior EV mechanic** at a small independent garage, two years into the trade.

She stays calm in the milder pictures and becomes **anxious** only when AGI comes in two years.
She dreams of a **worker-owned garage** and wants workers to share machine profits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build anything new.
